claims.text: At 4 a.m. on May 1, 1964, in the basement of College Hall at Dartmouth, John Kemeny and a student programmer typed RUN on neighbouring terminals and both got back correct answers to simple programs. Dartmouth’s own retrospective describes the scene as Dartmouth legend rather than as a documented record, and other accounts credit Kemeny and Thomas Kurtz jointly.

source.title: BASIC at Dartmouth, Dartmouth College — the institution’s own account of 1 May 1964

claims.text: The language was invented by John Kemeny and Thomas Kurtz. Kemeny began work on a draft of it in September 1963, having applied that year for a National Science Foundation grant to bring a GE-225 computer to campus and build a general-purpose time-sharing system; the grant was awarded despite referees’ serious doubts about staffing the work with undergraduates.

source.title: BASIC at Dartmouth, Dartmouth College — the institution’s own account of 1 May 1964

claims.text: The language ran on the Dartmouth Time-Sharing System, was implemented by undergraduate students, and opened to general users in June 1964. The original version had 14 statements and nine built-in functions.

source.title: Dartmouth BASIC: the Dartmouth Time-Sharing System, the original statement set, and its compile-and-go implementation

claims.text: By the autumn of 1964 hundreds of students were using it on 20 terminals around campus, and faculty across disciplines were supplied with teletypes and began writing their own programs.

source.title: BASIC at Dartmouth, Dartmouth College — the institution’s own account of 1 May 1964

claims.text: Unlike many of the later implementations that carried the name, the original was a compiler operating compile-and-go: it converted an entire program at once into machine code, rather than translating it line by line at each run.

source.title: Dartmouth BASIC: the Dartmouth Time-Sharing System, the original statement set, and its compile-and-go implementation

beats.broke: getting an answer out of a computer required a specialist and a batch turnaround, so anyone who was not a programmer was locked out of the machine entirely
beats.fix: a language small enough to learn in an afternoon, on a time-sharing system that returned the answer while you were still sitting at the terminal
beats.cost: the language was shaped by what a beginner could hold in mind, and later implementations kept the language while dropping the system that made it work
beats.interview: whether the language or the time-sharing system underneath it was the actual invention
